Day 1
From Hotel: 25 min → Tafawa Balewa Square
1.Tafawa Balewa Square
The historic outdoor square where Nigeria declared independence on October 1, 1960, named after the country's first Prime Minister, flanked by colonial-era grandstands and the former Lagos Race Course, now the site of national day celebrations.
Read more
Open 24/7

4 min · 2 min → National Museum Lagos
2.National Museum Lagos
Nigeria's foremost national museum, housing Benin bronze replicas, Nok terracotta figurines, and artifacts spanning 2,000 years of West African civilization, including ancient ironwork, colonial documents, and a permanent gallery on the Ife bronzes.

3.Freedom Park Lagos
A 19th-century colonial prison converted into a lush open-air cultural park, hosting live music, art exhibitions, and film screenings on the same grounds where political prisoners were once held — the iron cells and original perimeter wall still stand intact.

4.Holy Trinity Cathedral
Lagos's oldest surviving church, a Victorian Gothic Anglican cathedral built in 1867 on Broad Street, featuring original stained-glass windows, a soaring red-brick façade, and a bell tower that remains in active use for Sunday services.

Day 4
From Hotel: 1h 30min → Badagry Heritage Museum
1.Badagry Heritage Museum
The principal museum documenting the transatlantic slave trade in Southwest Nigeria, housing manacles, whips, slave ledgers, and over 500 artifacts alongside oral histories from Badagry's royal families who both facilitated and ultimately resisted the trade over two centuries.
Read more

2.Point of No Return
A monument on Badagry Beach marking the precise embarkation point where enslaved Africans were loaded onto ships bound for the Americas, reached by a short boat crossing from the Badagry waterfront and framed by an annual memorial ceremony held each October.

3.Seriki Abass Slave Barracoon
A 19th-century compound belonging to the Seriki Williams Abass slave-trading family, preserved with its underground cellar where enslaved people were held before embarkation — a low, narrow space requiring visitors to bend on entry — offering an unfiltered account of the trade's logistics.

4.First Storey Building in Nigeria
The oldest surviving two-story European-built structure in Nigeria, erected in 1845 by Wesleyan missionary Rev. Thomas Birch Freeman as a mission house, now maintained as a heritage site marking the earliest Western architectural footprint in the country.

Day 5
From Hotel: 30 min → Iga Idunganran
1.Iga Idunganran
The official residence of the Oba of Lagos, Yoruba Lagos's traditional ruler, first built in 1670 for Oba Gabaro and later refurbished with Portuguese-imported materials — a working royal palace that still hosts the annual Eyo festival and administrative functions of the Lagos throne.
Read more
Daily 6:00am - 11:00pm
~30 min
Advance permission is required to enter the palace itself; the gate and outer grounds are viewable without one
1 Iga Idunganran Street · Lagos Island
12 min · 5 min → Water House
2.Water House
A 19th-century Afro-Brazilian mansion built by Candido Da Rocha, one of the last of Lagos Island's Portuguese-Brazilian-style buildings still standing — named for the private well and Lagos's first freshwater fountain that once stood on the grounds, when Da Rocha sold water to a city with none.
Read more
Open 24/7
~20 min
Kakawa Street · Lagos Island
5 min · 3 min → Tinubu Square
3.Tinubu Square
A landscaped public square on Broad Street named for Madam Efunroye Tinubu, the 19th-century Lagos merchant and power broker, remodeled in 2017 around twin fountains, flowering trees and a life-size statue of Tinubu on a cenotaph — a formerly walled Independence Square turned everyday commercial crossroads.
Read more
Daily 9:00am - 9:00pm
~20 min
Broad Street · Lagos Island
4 min · 3 min → Central Mosque of Lagos
4.Central Mosque of Lagos
Lagos Island's principal mosque, opened in 1988 to replace an earlier 1913 building, its four minarets and gold-plated 15-meter central dome visible across the Lagos Island skyline — the seat of the Chief Imam of Lagos and the busiest Friday jumu'ah gathering point in the city.
Read more
Daily 8:00am - 6:00pm
~20 min
Free
Non-Muslim visitors are welcome outside prayer times; dress modestly and remove shoes before entering

1.Muri Okunola Park
A 2.7-acre landscaped park on Victoria Island, opened in 2008 on the site of the former Cloverleaf Park and named for a respected Nigerian High Court judge — manicured lawns, flower beds, shaded walking paths and rotating public artworks make it one of Lagos's most-visited green spaces.

2.Tarkwa Bay Beach
A sheltered, boat-only Atlantic beach formed by the breakwaters of Lagos Harbour, reached by a 20-minute water-taxi crossing from Five Cowries Terminal — calmer and cleaner than the Lekki Peninsula beaches, with a small resident fishing community, beach shacks and no road access at all.

Chowdeck

Best selection of upscale Nigerian cuisine in the VI corridor — asun, pepper soup, egusi, and jollof rice from quality kitchens. Menus are accurate, photos match reality, and refunds process quickly when items are missing.

Getting Around
Uber
Foreign number: accepted — the verification code reaches most international carriers via SMS.
The safest and most reliable option for visitors across Victoria Island, Lagos Island, Lekki, and Ikeja. Surge pricing applies on weekend evenings; avoid UberPool during rush hour as shared rides become very unpredictable in Lagos traffic.
uber.com
Bolt
Foreign number: accepted — the verification code reaches most international carriers via SMS.
Strong competitor to Uber across VI and Ikoyi with competitive pricing and high driver availability. Often faster to match than Uber on Victoria Island during peak periods. Negotiate with the driver before accepting if the route looks congested.
bolt.eu
Worth Knowing

Lagos traffic — Lagos traffic ranks among the worst globally. A 15-kilometer journey can take 20 minutes or 2 hours depending on the time of day. Plan activities outside peak hours — 7–10am outbound, 4–8pm return. Victoria Island to Lagos Island: 25–40 minutes off-peak, over an hour in rush hour. Day 4 — Badagry: depart by 7:30am to beat the worst of the outbound traffic.

Safety in Lagos — Victoria Island and Ikoyi are the safest areas for visitors and where most international hotels, restaurants, and attractions are concentrated. Avoid displaying expensive jewelry or phones in open markets. Use a registered Uber or Bolt rather than flagging taxis on the street. Badagry is safe for daytime visits; go with a guide.

Currency and cash — The Nigerian Naira — ₦, NGN — is the currency. ATMs are available across Victoria Island and accept international cards, though withdrawal limits are low at ₦20,000–₦40,000 per transaction. Carry some Naira cash for markets, suya vendors, and BRT. Most hotels and upscale restaurants accept Visa and Mastercard.

Dress in houses of worship — Holy Trinity Cathedral and other Lagos Island churches require covered shoulders and knees for entry. Carry a light scarf or overshirt when visiting religious sites.
